reasons.text: The fiscal gap between the budget bill's 0.6% of GDP, IFI's R$0.9 billion and Focus's -0.3% is unlikely to close before the December budget vote. The cheaper ways to meet the target (exclusions, or a target cut) push yields higher.
In em-macro's fit sample, bond moves after elections continued rather than reversed. The latest week added 204 bp at the long end while short rates barely moved, which is a term-premium shock.
Inflation expectations are drifting up (2027 IPCA at 4.34%), which caps any rally led by rate cuts.

resembles.why: As after the 2014 re-election, an incumbent left government won against the market's preference with a fiscal hole. Yields were set by doubts about whether the new term would adjust, not by the central bank.

bond.main_risk: A rapid, credible commitment to the 0.5% target and a spending freeze triggers a relief rally from yields that have already jumped.
bond.would_change: The budget passing without new exclusions, the Focus 2027 primary median rising toward the target, or a Copom hold with hawkish language that pulls 2027 inflation expectations down.

reasons.text: In em-macro's hold-out test, election currency moves continued, and fading them lost money on Brazil's 2022 run-off. The poll-surprise model that did hold up out of sample points the same way as the move.
The fiscal credibility gap is still open going into the budget vote and the 5 Jan inauguration.
Leveraged funds were crowded long the real before the vote and may still be unwinding. This badge is tested_no_lead, so it is supporting colour only.

resembles.why: After a re-election the market disliked, the real kept weakening while investors waited for proof of fiscal adjustment.

currency.main_risk: An orthodox signal from the government, or central bank swap supply beyond rollovers, sparks a 2003-style relief rally, helped by a hawkish Copom hold.
currency.would_change: USD/BRL returning below 5.0383, its pre-run-off level, together with Focus fiscal medians improving or a credible finance-team commitment to the target.

reasons.text: em-macro's spread-mispricing model is at best 1–3% better than 'no change' for Mexico, and not significantly so. There is no tested value signal to lean on.
The forces offset each other. US yields fell over the week and the auction yield dropped 10 bp, but the deficit target was loosened and Pemex support continues.
A Banxico hold is largely priced, and rate-surprise regressions add almost nothing out of sample. The 5 Nov decision is unlikely to break the tie.

resembles.why: As in 2025, the government is promising consolidation by squeezing capital spending and collecting more tax. This time the ambition has been scaled back, and the earlier target was missed.

bond.main_risk: A sustained US bond rally, or a dovish shift at Banxico, pulls Mbono yields down while we sit out.
bond.would_change: We would lean long if Banxico signals cuts while the US 10-year keeps falling and the budget passes without extra Pemex money. We would lean short if the budget adds spending or raises Pemex contributions above 81.1 billion pesos, or if a rating agency moves its outlook to negative.

reasons.text: Currency-mispricing signals for Mexico score 0.95–0.99 against 'no change', a slight edge that is not significant. That is too weak to justify a position.
Positioning is long the peso but not extreme, at the 73.7 percentile, and the gauge is tested with no lead. It gives no reliable contrarian signal.
The biggest risks to the peso are unscheduled US trade and security news, which can cut either way. Meanwhile the scheduled Banxico decision is priced for a hold.

resembles.why: No past episode fits well. The current mix of a priced central-bank hold, mild fiscal slippage and open-ended US trade risk has no close match in the episode list.

currency.main_risk: An unscheduled US announcement on USMCA or tariffs moves the peso sharply before we have a view.
currency.would_change: We would lean short the peso if the US proposes separate bilateral texts or talks of withdrawal, or if Banxico cuts by surprise. We would lean long if a USMCA round is scheduled with a constructive agenda and US tariffs on Mexican goods are reduced.

reasons.text: Near-term catalysts lean mildly toward narrowing. S&P has not downgraded from a stable outlook in 36 recorded actions, and an affirmation trims a tail. The budget's long-run base rate (19 of 21 on time) is well above the roughly 50% market price.

Against that, betting on mean reversion in France has failed out of sample. The spread widened for two years while models called it cheap, and it rose 15.2 bp in the latest month. The recent pattern of special laws in 2024 and 2025 also explains why the market sits near 50% rather than near 90.5%.
The level is stale: the last reading is a monthly average to 1 Sep, carrying an untested badge. A lean against an unknown starting point is not one we would bet on.

resembles.why: A minority government, a budget passed under threat of censure and rating pressure. In that episode the government fell on 4 December 2024 and the spread peaked at 88 bp, below where it already stands.

bond.main_risk: A censure vote brings down the government before the 10 Dec Article 47 deadline, widening the spread sharply while we stand aside.
bond.would_change: A fresh daily spread reading combined with a Socialist or Republican pledge not to censure the budget, or an S&P affirmation with a stable outlook, would tilt us to long (spread narrows). A censure motion gathering Socialist votes, or the government raising its 2026 deficit estimate, would tilt us to short.

reasons.text: EUR/USD is set mainly by US versus euro-area rates. The US 10-year at 5.05% against the Bund at 3.39% favours the dollar, but the US 2-year fell 14 bp over the week, so the direction is unclear.
The broad dollar barely moved over the week, and EUR/USD slipped only 0.28%. Neither shows a trend, and the EUR/USD series carries an untested badge.

The US midterms (3 Nov) and the FOMC decision (9 Dec) are two-way risks for the dollar. em-macro finds that rate decisions are mostly anticipated and that rate-surprise regressions add almost nothing out of sample.

resembles.why: No listed episode fits; French political crises have moved the spread far more than the euro.

currency.main_risk: A dovish Fed surprise on 9 Dec pulls US yields down and lifts the euro while we stand aside.
currency.would_change: A Fed signal on 9 Dec that cuts are coming, with US 2-year yields falling further, would point to long euro. A hawkish surprise, or French stress spilling into other euro-area spreads, would point to short.

reasons.text: Against gold: the 10-year real yield is high at 2.67%, the 10-year nominal is at 5.05%, and the 2-year above fed funds shows no easing priced.
Against gold: central-bank purchases fell to 20.34 tonnes from 45.76, and geopolitical risk eased to 165.253 from 220.838.

For gold: real yields fell 9 bp and the 2-year fell 14 bp over the week. With the midterms on 3 Nov and the FOMC on 9 Dec, the rate backdrop could turn friendlier. The only quantitative forecast, the unscored model, is close to zero.

resembles.why: Real yields were strongly positive while central banks were still buying heavily. Gold rose for a month and then fell over six months, as rates won out over official demand. Today's mix of high real yields and wobbling official purchases is similar, but the Fed is holding rather than hiking, so the fit is loose.

gold.main_risk: Standing aside misses a large move. A midterm or FOMC shock that pulls real yields sharply down, or a geopolitical spike, could lift gold quickly. Alternatively, a further collapse in central-bank buying could expose gold to its high-real-yield headwind.
gold.would_change: Lean long if the 10-year real yield keeps falling below 2.67% after the 9 Dec FOMC and the next IMF data show purchases recovering toward August's 45.76 tonnes. Lean short if real yields rise back above the week-ago 2.76% and another month shows official buying near or below September's 20.34 tonnes.
